subject: Fitting a simple CFA model on a correlation matrix

messages.author: 09c3aafdd465cbaa
messages.subject: Fitting a simple CFA model on a correlation matrix
parts:
Dear lavaan contributors,

I’m currently working on fitting a simple CFA model (4 observed variables, 1 latent variable) using the correlation matrix of the observed variables.

In reviewing literature (e.g., Cudeck, 1989), I’ve come across discussions about the potential issues with fitting non-scale-invariant models on correlation matrices. 

I’m wondering if anyone could offer insights or recommend resources to clarify whether using a correlation matrix in the cfa() function in lavaan might affect the accuracy of the omnibus test statistic or standard errors.

Here is the code I’m using:

model <- 'LV1 =~ MV1 + MV2 + MV3 + MV4'
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, sample.cov=COR.matrix, std.lv=T, sample.nobs = 250)

Thank you very much for your help.

Kind regards,

Laura

REF: Cudeck, R. (1989). Analysis of correlation matrices using covariance structure models. Psychological bulletin, 105(2), 317.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Fitting a simple CFA model on a correlation matrix
parts:
Hello Laura,

Recent versions of lavaan now have a correlation = TRUE option, which
allows for the analysis of correlation matrices. Only the GLS and WLS
estimators are supported. (I don't think it is possible using ML, but I
may be wrong).

What happens behind the scenes:

1) the 'residual' variances of the indicators are no longer 'free'
parameters; their values are set so that the total variance is one

2) the 'Gamma' matrix (normal-based, or ADF) is modified to reflect the
sampling variability of the elements in a correlation matrix (excluding
the unit diagonal)

This should lead to correct standard errors for the model parameters,
and 'robust' fit measures.

I should perhaps add that this 'feature' is relatively new/experimental,
and more simulation studies are needed to verify that it works correctly.

As for literature: there is not much. But there is this book chapter:

Bentler, P. and Savalei, V. (2010). Analysis of correlation structures:
current status and open problems. In "Statistics in the Social
Sciences', edited by Kolenikov S., Steinley, D, Thombs, L.

(I can send you a pdf offline; just email me).

Yves.
